items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So, he talked to Earl Hood and Earl Hood gave me a chance to play in his band.

ctx.x: Did your mother live in Columbus her whole life?

Oh yeah, when she left Kentucky, she left for good. She left there when I was six months old and she stayed. She did come back to see me just about every year but one time she was called, I was very sick. I had typhoid, and at that time there was no antidote for typhoid fever. I don’t know how I attracted it, I was about eight years old or nine years old, but the fever was just doing me in and the doctor had given me up. He said I’ve tried everything as a country doctor that he knew. So my grandmother, the one…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: So I went to rehearsal and Earl Hood liked me so I joined the band.

ctx.x: fantastic saxophone player, he -- oh, Johnny Hodges knew him well, everybody, because he was really a good saxophone player. He moved next door to my mother and I used to play and play, you know, try to be a trumpet player. So he heard me one day he said -- he was playing with Earl Hood. He said, "Why don't you come to rehearsal."

So I went to rehearsal and Earl Hood liked me so I joined the band. And we had a job on Saturday nights, you know, just around Columbus, Chillicothe, Ohio, someplace. And my mother bought me a tuxedo and everything. And, of course, we got paid, it was only about 35 cents or 50 cents, very seldom $1.00, you know. But he wouldn't pay me. He'd say, well, you're playing for experience, see.

So I'd come home, I'd be so sleepy on Monday I wouldn't have my homework done. And my mother would ask me -- well, she had gotten married then, I had a stepfather. And she would ask my stepfather, "Don't you think he should be getting some money?" He said, "Well, he's playing like everybody else." So she asked me, says, "What do you do with the money?"
